title: Failover surge protocol summary
content:
Summary:

This is a working summary of the surge/failover protocol we should use during region-level degradations (partial or full region outage) where traffic must be shifted across regions and DNS-based routing adjustments are required. Aim: limit user-facing errors, keep tail latency bounded, and avoid double-cost amplification (over-provisioning + burst) during incident.

High-level goals:
- Fast decision path for on-call to bring up warm standby and move traffic.
- Clear verification steps to avoid cache-warmup storms or negative feedback loops.
- Conservative DNS TTL and staged shift (canary -> ramp -> full) with automatic rollback criteria.
- Pre-approved infra commands/snippets to run in the heat of the moment.

Context / assumptions:
- Primary region: us-central1 (GCP). Secondary standby: us-east1 (GCP) + aws-eu-west-1 as tertiary.
- DNS is managed in Route53 for customer-facing apex; Cloud DNS also used for some internal endpoints.
- Traffic routing uses an NLB + GlobalLB with healthchecks + Route53 weighted routing.
- Warm standby cluster(s) exist for replicas of inference-serving pools but are typically scaled to 10-20% of normal capacity to save cost.
- KV cache (prefix cache + user KV) is not globally replicated in real-time. We must expect cache-miss spike.

Fast checklist (for on-call):
1) Confirm region health: check cloud console, GCP status, internal tracing dashboards.
   - Metric quick hits: region CPU/GPU saturation, API 5xx rate, regional SLO-err budget burn, global request error rate.
2) Notify stakeholders: #sre-oncall, #eng-infra, product oncall (if >15m). Post short summary + link to incident channel.
3) Activate warm-standby scale policy: run infra snippet to increase replica count to X (recommended: from 20% -> 50%).
   - Example (terraform/az cli): run `./scripts/scale-standby --region us-east1 --pool inference--prod --target-pct 50` (idempotent).
4) Reduce DNS TTL (if not already low): set apex TTL -> 30s (note: Route53 minimum change propagation caveats).
5) Canary traffic: shift 5-10% weight to standby via Route53 weighted entries. Verify health on canary.
6) Observe for 2 min: check tail latency, error rate, GPU queue lengths. If canary stable, proceed to 25% then 50%.
7) Ramp to 100% only if metrics stable for at least 5 minutes per step.
8) After full shift, keep standby at scaled level for 30–60 minutes while monitoring; don’t aggressively downscale cache primed instances unless certain traffic patterns resume.

Verification/observability details:
- Dashboards to watch: per-region 99th latency, 5xx/sec, request queue backlog, GPU-util, token-per-sec.
- Traces: look for long KV fetch durations; new-region users will have higher first-token latencies.
- Logs: tail error logs for auth failures (region-blocked keys), or CORS/edge errors caused by new edge route.
- CDN: invalidate short-lived edges if A records change and stale edge content is problematic.

DNS specifics and gotchas:
- Route53 weighted routing: updates are quick but clients may cache answers beyond TTL; reducing TTL helps but doesn’t guarantee immediate switch for every client.
- DO NOT delete primary records — prefer adjusting weights so we can rollback fast.
- If using global loadbalancer with health checks, failing nodes will be removed; ensure healthcheck endpoints are functional from both regions.
- If customer networks use long-lived resolvers (corporate), they might respect TTLs poorly — include CST/enterprise comms for large customers if outage is long.

Cache and downstream state:
- Expect cold-start of KV cache and LRU thrash. Consider rolling cache warmups: route 5% of traffic with warm cache keys (repeat requests) to prepopulate critical prefixes.
- For sessions: if sticky session tokens are region-bound, rotate session tokens gracefully — issue new global tokens when switching.
- Database replicas often lag — avoid writes that assume zero replication lag. For customer-facing operations that require strict consistency, fail back to primary after recovery.

Canary procedure (detailed):
- Step A: set Route53 weight standby=10, primary=90. TTL=30s.
- Step B: run smoke test suite against standby (30 synthetic requests that exercise long-context and tool calling). Look for error rate <0.2% and 99th latency < 2x baseline.
- Step C: confirm SLOs on real traffic via sampling (set a 1/100 sample routed to tracing pipeline prefixed with `failover-canary`).
- Step D: if canary passes, increase to 25% and repeat quickValidation. If fails at any step, revert to primary by restoring weights and TTL.

Rollback criteria (when to abort and switch back):
- Any spike of 5xx to >1% of regional traffic sustained for >2 minutes.
- GPU queue > target threshold (e.g., 500 pending tokens) for >3 minutes.
- External dependencies failing (DB read errors, third-party auth) that cause a class of requests to error.
- Large increase in cost projection (uncontrolled autoscaling causing 3x expected spend) and product owner explicit decision.

Warm-standby warmup tips:
- Pre-pull model weights on standby GPUs during lower-traffic windows (cron weekly) to reduce load time.
- Keep a small fleet of pre-quantized replicas to reduce load-time jitter.
- Maintain a small pre-warmed KV snapshot (top-N prefixes) refreshed every 10 minutes.
- Run a periodic ‘safepoke’ synthetic workload to keep model kernels cached and avoid cold CPU/GPU JIT stalls.

Operational snippets (for copy/paste):
- Scale standby pool (kubernetes example):
  kubectl --context=us-east1 scale deployment inference-pool --replicas=40 -n prod || echo "scale failed"
- Update Route53 weight (aws cli):
  aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id ZZZ --change-batch '{"Changes":[{"Action":"UPSERT","ResourceRecordSet":{"Name":"api.redwood.example","Type":"A","SetIdentifier":"us-east1-weighted","Weight":10,"AliasTarget":{...}}}]}'
- Healthcheck quick: curl -sS https://us-east1-pool.health/redwood | jq .status  # expect OK

Post-incident tasks (to add to runbook after event):
- Capture a timeline of actions with timestamps + who executed each step.
- Measure user-impacted requests and quantify SLO burn.
- Collect root cause: why primary degraded? infra? overload? software bug?
- Cost accounting: incremental cost of failover (scales + egress + extra GPU-hours).
- Update runbook steps that were ambiguous or required improvisation.

Notes to self / unresolved questions (items to action outside incident):
- Do we want an automated short-circuit for TTL drop to 10s on detection of region-wide healthcheck failures? Risk: might amplify DNS churn.
- Should we keep third region (aws-eu-west-1) warmed at 5% baseline for geographic fanout during long incidents? Cost vs benefit analysis needed.
- Improve synthetic suite to include heavy stateful sessions to emulate long-context workloads; current smoke tests are too light.
- Add a documented approval matrix for doing full 100% shift (who signs off beyond SRE lead).

Appendix: quick links and references
- Incident channel: #sre-oncall
- Infra repo PR for scaling scripts: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/987
- Related ticket: JIRA-OPS-4123 (warm-standby economics)
- Previous postmortem reference: regional-failover-execution-retrospective-q1-2025 (see lessons about cache thrash)

End of draft.

(If this doc was used during an incident, append a short timeline under 'event_log' with who executed which snippet and timestamps)
